blocks.body:
The rational numbers are built from the integers by allowing division by every nonzero integer. Nothing stops us from being more selective. We could allow only powers of $10$ as denominators and get the decimal fractions $n/10^k$; or allow only denominators not divisible by $3$, and get a ring in which $2$, $4$, $5$ and $7$ have become invertible but $3$ has not. Localisation is this construction carried out in an arbitrary commutative ring: choose a set $S$ of elements you would like to be units, and form the ring $S^{-1}A$ of fractions with denominators in $S$.

The name comes from geometry. If $A$ is a ring of polynomial functions on some space and $a$ is a point, a fraction $f/g$ with $g(a) \ne 0$ is not defined everywhere, but it is a perfectly good function on the region near $a$ where $g$ does not vanish. Allowing all such denominators gives the ring of functions that make sense near $a$, the ring of functions local to $a$. Chevalley, who in 1944 defined the ring of quotients of a Noetherian ring with respect to a multiplicative set, described the quotient $A/\mathfrak p$ as the ring of the subvariety cut out by a prime $\mathfrak p$, and the localised ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$ as the right tool for studying a neighbourhood of that subvariety.

Two facts make localisation indispensable. First, it is exact: it carries exact sequences of modules to exact sequences, so it can be applied to kernels, images and quotients without loss. Second, it detects things: a module is zero if all its localisations at maximal ideals are zero, and many properties (being reduced, a map being injective, a module being projective, a ring being regular or Cohen-Macaulay) can be tested one prime at a time. So a problem about $A$ can be cut into many problems about local rings, which have their own tools, Nakayama's lemma first among them ([[local-rings]]). In the papers this page prepares for, localisation is constantly used and rarely stated: Guan and Hu formalise regular and Cohen-Macaulay rings through their localisations, Lombardi turns local-global arguments into explicit computations with finitely many comaximal elements, and Xu rebuilds affine schemes over $\mathbb F_1$ starting from the universal property of $S^{-1}A$.

This page builds the construction, explains why it has the shape it has, describes the ideals and primes of a localisation and what localisation preserves, localises modules, and proves the local-global principles that research papers use without comment. It ends with the structure sheaf of an affine scheme, which is assembled from localisations. We use the language of [[noetherian-rings]] and [[modules]], and [[tensor-products]] for the base-change description of $S^{-1}M$; rings are commutative with $1$, and ring maps send $1$ to $1$.

blocks.title: Fractions with chosen denominators
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a ring. To divide by elements of a set $S$ we must also be able to divide by their products, and dividing by $1$ should change nothing. This forces the first definition.

In an integral domain one can simply work inside the field of fractions: $S^{-1}A$ is the set of all $a/s \in \operatorname{Frac}(A)$ with $a \in A$, $s \in S$, a subring with $A \subseteq S^{-1}A \subseteq \operatorname{Frac}(A)$. This is how number theorists usually meet it. For rings with zero divisors there is no ambient field, and the fractions have to be built by hand as equivalence classes of pairs. The surprise is that the familiar rule $a/s = b/t \iff at = bs$ no longer works and must be weakened by an extra factor.

blocks.title: Multiplicative set and ring of fractions
blocks.body:
A subset $S \subseteq A$ is multiplicative (or multiplicatively closed) if $1 \in S$ and $st \in S$ whenever $s, t \in S$.

On the set of pairs $A \times S$ define
$$\begin{aligned}(a, s) \sim (b, t) \iff{}& \text{there is } u \in S\\ &\text{with } u(at - bs) = 0 .\end{aligned}$$
Write $a/s$ for the class of $(a, s)$ and $S^{-1}A$ for the set of classes. With
$$\frac{a}{s} + \frac{b}{t} = \frac{at + bs}{st}, \qquad \frac{a}{s}\cdot\frac{b}{t} = \frac{ab}{st},$$
$S^{-1}A$ is a ring with zero $0/1$ and identity $1/1$, and $\iota\colon A \to S^{-1}A$, $a \mapsto a/1$, is a ring homomorphism. It is called the localisation of $A$ at $S$ (also the ring of fractions or ring of quotients of $A$ with respect to $S$). Each $s \in S$ becomes a unit: $(s/1)(1/s) = s/s = 1/1$.

blocks.title: The relation is an equivalence and the operations are well defined
blocks.body: For a multiplicative set $S \subseteq A$, the relation $\sim$ on $A \times S$ is an equivalence relation, and the sum and product of classes do not depend on the representatives chosen. Every fraction can be expanded: $a/s = (ua)/(us)$ for every $u \in S$.

Reflexivity and symmetry are clear (take $u = 1$, and note $u(at-bs)=0$ iff $u(bs-at)=0$).

Transitivity is where the factor $u$ is needed. Suppose $u(at - bs) = 0$ and $v(br - ct) = 0$ with $u, v \in S$; we want $(a, s) \sim (c, r)$. Multiply the first equation by $vr$ and the second by $us$ and add:
$$\begin{aligned}0 &= uv(atr - bsr) + uv(bsr - cst)\\ &= uv\,t\,(ar - cs) .\end{aligned}$$
Since $w = uvt \in S$, this says $w(ar - cs) = 0$, as required. Note that we had to multiply by $t$, and $t$ may be a zero divisor; that is why the relation must allow a factor from $S$.

Well-definedness. It suffices to change one fraction at a time, say replace $(a, s)$ by an equivalent $(a', s')$ with $u(as' - a's) = 0$, keeping $(b, t)$. For the product,
$$\begin{aligned}&u\big((ab)(s't) - (a'b)(st)\big)\\ &\qquad= u\,bt\,(as' - a's) = 0,\end{aligned}$$
so $(ab, st) \sim (a'b, s't)$. For the sum,
$$\begin{aligned}&u\big((at + bs)s't - (a't + bs')st\big)\\ &\qquad= u\,t^2(as' - a's) = 0,\end{aligned}$$
so $(at + bs, st) \sim (a't + bs', s't)$. Changing the second fraction is the same computation with the roles exchanged. The ring axioms are then inherited from $A$, since every identity among fractions can be checked after bringing them to a common denominator. Finally $(ua)s - a(us) = 0$ gives $a/s = ua/us$.

blocks.body: Why not just use $at = bs$? Without the extra factor the relation is not transitive once $S$ contains zero divisors. In $A = \mathbb R[x,y]/(xy)$ with $S = \{1, x, x^2, \dots\}$ we have $y\cdot x - 0\cdot 1 = 0$, so naively $y/1 \sim 0/x$; and $0/x \sim 0/1$. But $y\cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 1 = y \ne 0$, so the naive relation does not identify $y/1$ with $0/1$. The correct relation does: $u = x$ gives $x(y\cdot 1 - 0\cdot 1) = 0$. Geometrically this is the picture above: $x$ is invertible near $(1,0)$, and there $y$ is the zero function. When $A$ is a domain and $0 \notin S$, the factor $u$ can be cancelled and the naive rule is correct.

blocks.title: Points of the two axes
blocks.body: Let $A = \mathbb R[x,y]/(xy)$ and $\mathfrak p = (x - 1)$. Show that $y \in \mathfrak p$, that $\mathfrak p$ is a maximal ideal, and that $A_{\mathfrak p} \cong \mathbb R[x]_{(x-1)}$, the ring of rational functions in one variable defined at $x = 1$. (This is Gathmann's Exercise 6.13(a), and the algebra behind the figure: near $(1,0)$ the space looks like the $x$-axis.)
blocks.solution:
In $A$ we have $y = -y(x - 1) + xy = -y(x-1)$, so $y \in (x-1)$. Hence $\mathfrak p = (x-1, y)$ and $A/\mathfrak p \cong \mathbb R[x,y]/(xy, x-1, y) \cong \mathbb R$, a field, so $\mathfrak p$ is maximal.

In $A_{\mathfrak p}$ the element $x$ is a unit because $x 
otin \mathfrak p$ (its image in $A/\mathfrak p = \mathbb R$ is $1$). From $xy = 0$ we get $y/1 = (x y)/x = 0$. Consider the map $\mathbb R[x] 	o A_{\mathfrak p}$. Every element of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is $g/h$ with $g, h$ polynomials in $x, y$ and $h 
otin \mathfrak p$; since $y/1 = 0$, we may replace $g$ and $h$ by $g(x,0)$ and $h(x,0)$, and $h 
otin \mathfrak p$ means $h(1,0)

Conversely, the ring map $A 	o \mathbb R[x]_{(x-1)}$, $x \mapsto x$, $y \mapsto 0$ (well defined since $xy \mapsto 0$) sends every element outside $\mathfrak p$ to a polynomial not vanishing at $1$, hence to a unit, so by the universal property proved in the next section it extends to $A_{\mathfrak p} 	o \mathbb R[x]_{(x-1)}$. The two maps are inverse to each other on generators, so $A_{\mathfrak p} \cong \mathbb R[x]_{(x-1)}$. The same computation at $(0,1)$ gives the $y$-axis instead; at the origin, $\mathfrak m = (x, y)$, neither $x$ nor $y$ is inverted, and $A_{\mathfrak m}$ still sees both branches.

blocks.title: The standard localisations
blocks.body:
The following choices of $S$ occur constantly; the notation is as in the Stacks Project and Gathmann.

1. Powers of one element: $S = \{1, f, f^2, \dots\}$ gives $A_f$, also written $A[1/f]$. Its elements are $a/f^n$.
2. Complement of a prime: if $\mathfrak p$ is a prime ideal, $S = A \setminus \mathfrak p$ is multiplicative (this is exactly the definition of prime), and $A_{\mathfrak p} = (A \setminus \mathfrak p)^{-1}A$ is the localisation at $\mathfrak p$. Its elements are $a/s$ with $s \notin \mathfrak p$. Note what is inverted: everything outside $\mathfrak p$, not $\mathfrak p$ itself.
3. Non-zero-divisors: the set of all non-zero-divisors is multiplicative, and the localisation is the total ring of fractions $Q(A)$. For a domain this is the field of fractions $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$; it is the largest $S$ for which $A \to S^{-1}A$ is injective.
4. For a module $M$ the same letters are used: $M_f$, $M_{\mathfrak p}$ (see the section on modules).

For the integers: $\mathbb Z_{(p)} = \{a/b : p \nmid b\}$ is the localisation at the prime $(p)$; $\mathbb Z[1/p] = \{a/p^n\}$ inverts $p$ only; $\mathbb Z[1/10]$ is the ring of decimal fractions; $(\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\})^{-1}\mathbb Z = \mathbb Q$.

blocks.title: Kernel of the localisation map
blocks.body:
Let $S \subseteq A$ be multiplicative and $\iota\colon A \to S^{-1}A$, $a \mapsto a/1$.

1. $\ker \iota = \{a \in A : sa = 0 \text{ for some } s \in S\}$.
2. $\iota$ is injective if and only if $S$ contains no zero divisors.
3. $S^{-1}A = 0$ if and only if $0 \in S$. In particular $A_f = 0$ if and only if $f$ is nilpotent.

1. $a/1 = 0/1$ means $u(a\cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 1) = ua = 0$ for some $u \in S$.

2. If some $s \in S$ is a zero divisor, say $sa = 0$ with $a \ne 0$, then $a \in \ker\iota$ by (1). Conversely if no element of $S$ kills a nonzero element, the kernel in (1) is zero.

3. $S^{-1}A = 0$ means $1/1 = 0/1$, i.e. $u\cdot 1 = 0$ for some $u \in S$, i.e. $0 \in S$. For $S = \{f^n\}$ this says $f^n = 0$ for some $n$.

blocks.title: Localising a finite ring
blocks.body: Compute $(\mathbb Z/12)_2$, the localisation of $A = \mathbb Z/12$ at $S = \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$ (the powers of $2$ modulo $12$; note $16 \equiv 4$). Find the kernel of $A \to A_2$, and show $A_2 \cong \mathbb Z/3$.
blocks.solution:
By the theorem the kernel consists of the $a$ killed by some power of $2$. In $\mathbb Z/12$, $2^ka \equiv 0 \pmod{12}$ with $k \ge 2$ holds iff $3 \mid a$, and $2a \equiv 0$ iff $6 \mid a$. So $\ker = \{0, 3, 6, 9\} = 3\mathbb Z/12$.

Next, every fraction is of the form $a/1$. Indeed $4/1$ is a unit of $A_2$ (it lies in the image of $S$), and $4 \cdot 4 = 16 \equiv 4$, so $e = 4/1$ satisfies $e^2 = e$; multiplying by $e^{-1}$ gives $e = 1$. Thus $1/4 = 1$ and $1/2 = 2/4 = 2/1$, and every fraction equals some $a/1$. So $A_2$ is the image of $A$, which is $A/\ker = (\mathbb Z/12)/(3) \cong \mathbb Z/3$. Concretely $A_2$ has three elements, $0, 1/1, 2/1$, and $1/2 = 2/1$ because $2 \cdot 2 = 4 \equiv 1 \pmod 3$. This matches the Chinese remainder decomposition $\mathbb Z/12 \cong \mathbb Z/4 \times \mathbb Z/3$: inverting $2$ kills the factor $\mathbb Z/4$, in which $2$ is nilpotent, and leaves $\mathbb Z/3$, in which $2$ is already a unit. A brute-force count of the classes of $A\times S$ (see the checks) confirms three classes.

blocks.title: Representatives in a local ring of the integers
blocks.body: In $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, is $9/3$ an element? Is $1/3$?
blocks.solution: $9/3 = 3/1$, because $9 \cdot 1 - 3 \cdot 3 = 0$. So $9/3$ is an element of $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$ even though it is written with a denominator divisible by $3$: membership means that some representative has a denominator prime to $3$. On the other hand $1/3$ is not in $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$: if $1/3 = a/b$ with $3 \nmid b$, then $b = 3a$, a contradiction. In general $x \in \mathbb Q$ lies in $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ exactly when $v_p(x) \ge 0$, where $v_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation (the exponent of $p$ in $x$).

2. (Basic) Compute $(\mathbb Z/12)_3$ and $(\mathbb Z/12)_6$. Which factor of $\mathbb Z/4 \times \mathbb Z/3$ survives in each?

blocks.title: The universal property and other definitions
blocks.body: The construction by pairs is concrete but clumsy: checking that a map out of $S^{-1}A$ is well defined means checking compatibility with $\sim$ every time. Almost every text therefore proves, right after the construction, that $S^{-1}A$ is characterised by a mapping property, and then uses only that property. Vakil goes further and remarks that it is cleaner to take the universal property as the definition, prove that something satisfying it exists, and derive everything else from it.

blocks.title: Universal property of localisation
blocks.body:
Let $S \subseteq A$ be multiplicative and let $\varphi\colon A \to B$ be a ring map such that $\varphi(s)$ is a unit of $B$ for every $s \in S$. Then there is exactly one ring map $\psi\colon S^{-1}A \to B$ with $\psi(a/1) = \varphi(a)$ for all $a$, namely
$$\psi(a/s) = \varphi(a)\varphi(s)^{-1}.$$
Consequently, if $\iota'\colon A \to C$ is another ring map inverting $S$ with the same property, there is a unique isomorphism $S^{-1}A \cong C$ compatible with the maps from $A$.

Existence. The formula is well defined: if $u(at - bs) = 0$ then applying $\varphi$ gives $\varphi(u)(\varphi(a)\varphi(t) - \varphi(b)\varphi(s)) = 0$, and since $\varphi(u), \varphi(s), \varphi(t)$ are units, $\varphi(a)\varphi(s)^{-1} = \varphi(b)\varphi(t)^{-1}$. It respects sums and products because the formulas for fractions are the usual ones and $\varphi$ is a ring map, and $\psi(a/1) = \varphi(a)$.

Uniqueness. If $\psi'$ is another such map, then $\psi'(1/s)\varphi(s) = \psi'(1/s)\psi'(s/1) = \psi'(1) = 1$, so $\psi'(1/s) = \varphi(s)^{-1}$, and $\psi'(a/s) = \psi'(a/1)\psi'(1/s) = \varphi(a)\varphi(s)^{-1}$.

Uniqueness of $S^{-1}A$. Given $C$ with the same property, we get maps $S^{-1}A \to C$ and $C \to S^{-1}A$ under $A$. Their composite $S^{-1}A \to S^{-1}A$ is a map under $A$, and so is the identity; by the uniqueness part they agree. The same holds for the other composite, so both maps are isomorphisms. This is the standard argument that an object defined by a universal property is unique up to unique isomorphism.

blocks.title: What is $S^{-1}A$?

items.label: Fractions
items.body: Pairs $(a, s)$ modulo $u(at - bs) = 0$, with the school rules for adding and multiplying fractions. This is the definition in the Stacks Project, Gathmann, Sutherland and Atiyah-Macdonald, and it is the one needed whenever an explicit computation is made, for instance to find the kernel of $A \to S^{-1}A$.

items.label: Universal property
items.body: $S^{-1}A$ is the initial $A$-algebra in which the elements of $S$ become units: a ring map $A \to S^{-1}A$ through which every $S$-inverting map factors uniquely. Vakil recommends this as the definition; the fraction construction then becomes a proof of existence (his Exercise 2.3.A asks to verify that the fractions satisfy it).

items.label: Three checkable properties
items.body: A ring map $f\colon A \to B$ is a localisation at $S$ if and only if (i) $f(s)$ is a unit for all $s \in S$, (ii) every element of $B$ has the form $f(a)f(s)^{-1}$, and (iii) $\ker f$ consists of the $a$ with $sa = 0$ for some $s \in S$. Buzzard reports that this characterisation, suggested by Neil Strickland, is the one Mathlib uses; unlike the universal property it does not quantify over all rings $B$, so it can be checked on a given model.

items.label: Subring of the fraction field
items.body: For an integral domain $A$ and $0 \notin S$, $S^{-1}A$ is simply $\{a/s\} \subseteq \operatorname{Frac}(A)$, so $A \subseteq S^{-1}A \subseteq \operatorname{Frac}(A)$; the extra factor $u$ is invisible. This is the working definition in algebraic number theory.

items.label: Chevalley's two steps
items.body:
For a Noetherian ring $o$ and multiplicative $S

When $S$ is the complement of a prime, the result is a local ring. Chevalley shows (his Proposition 1) that his ideal is the intersection of the primary components $\mathfrak q_i$ of an irredundant decomposition of $0$ whose primes $\mathfrak p_i$ miss $S$. One checks (this comparison is not in his paper) that this ideal is exactly the kernel $\{a : sa = 0 	ext{ for some } s\in S\}$ of the modern map: if $sa = 0$ with $s 
otin \mathfrak p_i$ then $a \in \mathfrak q_i$ because $\mathfrak q_i$ is primary; conversely, choosing $s_j \in \mathfrak p_j \cap S$ with $s_j^n \in \mathfrak q_j$ for the other components, $s = \prod s_j^n$ kills $a$. So for Noetherian rings the two constructions agree.

blocks.body: Five sources, five definitions of the same ring. They agree up to unique isomorphism, by the universal property.

blocks.title: Strickland's characterisation
blocks.body: A ring map $f\colon A \to B$ is isomorphic under $A$ to $\iota\colon A \to S^{-1}A$ if and only if it satisfies conditions (i), (ii), (iii) of the third view above.

The map $\iota$ satisfies (i) and (ii) by construction ($a/s = \iota(a)\iota(s)^{-1}$), and (iii) by the kernel theorem of the previous section; isomorphisms under $A$ preserve the three conditions. Conversely, assume (i)-(iii). By (i) and the universal property there is $\psi\colon S^{-1}A \to B$ with $\psi(a/s) = f(a)f(s)^{-1}$. By (ii) it is surjective. If $\psi(a/s) = 0$ then $f(a) = 0$, so by (iii) $ua = 0$ for some $u \in S$, and then $a/s = ua/us = 0$. So $\psi$ is injective, hence an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Adjoining an inverse
blocks.body: For $f \in A$ there is an isomorphism $A[x]/(fx - 1) \cong A_f$ sending $x$ to $1/f$.

Let $C = A[x]/(fx - 1)$ with the evident map $A \to C$. In $C$ the element $f$ has inverse $x$, so $C$ inverts $S = \{f^n\}$. If $\varphi\colon A \to B$ is a ring map with $\varphi(f)$ a unit, the map $A[x] \to B$ extending $\varphi$ by $x \mapsto \varphi(f)^{-1}$ kills $fx - 1$, so it induces $C \to B$; it is the only map under $A$, because $x$ must go to the inverse of $\varphi(f)$. So $C$ has the universal property of $A_f$, and by uniqueness $C \cong A_f$ with $x \mapsto 1/f$. This is Gathmann's Exercise 6.13(b).

blocks.title: Localisation in stages
blocks.body:
Let $S, T \subseteq A$ be multiplicative and let $\bar T$ be the image of $T$ in $S^{-1}A$. Then $ST = \{st\}$ is multiplicative and
$$(ST)^{-1}A \cong \bar T^{-1}(S^{-1}A).$$
In particular $(A_f)_{g/1} \cong A_{fg}$, and if $\mathfrak q \subseteq \mathfrak p$ are primes then $(A_{\mathfrak p})_{\mathfrak q A_{\mathfrak p}} \cong A_{\mathfrak q}$.

A ring map $\varphi\colon A \to B$ inverts $ST$ if and only if it inverts both $S$ and $T$: one direction because $s = s\cdot 1$ and $t = 1\cdot t$ lie in $ST$, the other because a product of units is a unit, and if $\varphi(st)$ is a unit then so are its factors. Maps $\bar T^{-1}(S^{-1}A) \to B$ correspond, by the universal property twice, to maps $S^{-1}A \to B$ inverting $\bar T$, hence to maps $A \to B$ inverting $S$ and $T$. Maps $(ST)^{-1}A \to B$ correspond to maps $A \to B$ inverting $ST$. Both rings therefore have the same universal property and are uniquely isomorphic.

For $A_f$ and $g$: the multiplicative set generated by $f$ and $g$ is $\{f^ag^b\}$, and inverting it is the same as inverting $\{(fg)^n\}$, because $fg$ is invertible exactly when $f$ and $g$ are. For primes $\mathfrak q \subseteq \mathfrak p$ take $S = A \setminus \mathfrak p$ and $T = A \setminus \mathfrak q$. Then $S \subseteq T$, so $ST = T$ and $(ST)^{-1}A = A_{\mathfrak q}$. It remains to see that inverting $\bar T$ in $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is the same as inverting $A_{\mathfrak p} \setminus \mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}$. An element of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ outside $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}$ has the form $t/s$ with $t \notin \mathfrak q$ (if $t \in \mathfrak q$ the fraction lies in $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}$), and $t/s = (t/1)(1/s)$ with $1/s$ already a unit; so a map inverting $\bar T$ inverts all of $A_{\mathfrak p} \setminus \mathfrak q A_{\mathfrak p}$, and conversely $\bar T$ lies in that set. The two universal properties coincide.

blocks.title: Saturation
blocks.body: The saturation of a multiplicative set $S$ is $\hat S = \{a \in A : ab \in S \text{ for some } b \in A\}$, the set of divisors of elements of $S$; equivalently, the set of $a$ whose image in $S^{-1}A$ is a unit. $S$ is saturated if $S = \hat S$. Then $\hat S$ is multiplicative, $S^{-1}A \cong \hat S^{-1}A$, and two multiplicative sets give isomorphic localisations (under $A$) exactly when they have the same saturation. Complements of primes are saturated; Lombardi notes that, among saturated sets, these are exactly the ones whose localisation is a nonzero local ring.

blocks.title: The saturation of the powers of 2
blocks.body: In $\mathbb Z$, find the saturation of $S = \{1, 2, 4, 8, \dots\}$. Compare with the multiplicative set $\{\pm\alpha^n\}$ that Coykendall and Kettinger use to define $D[1/\alpha]$.
blocks.solution: If $ab = 2^n$ then by unique factorisation $a = \pm 2^k$ with $k \le n$. Conversely each $\pm 2^k$ divides a power of $2$. So $\hat S = \{\pm 2^k : k \ge 0\}$, and $\mathbb Z[1/2] = \hat S^{-1}\mathbb Z$: inverting $2$ automatically inverts $-2$. Coykendall and Kettinger localise a ring of integers at $\{\pm\alpha^n\}$ and write the result $D[1/\alpha]$; including the sign changes nothing, since $-1$ is already a unit. Coykendall and Kettinger also describe their set as the complement of the union of the primes not containing $\alpha$; strictly, that complement is the saturation of $\{\pm\alpha^n\}$, which gives the same ring. In general the saturation of $S$ is the complement of the union of the primes disjoint from $S$. Indeed, if $ab = s \in S$ then every prime containing $a$ contains $s$, so $a$ lies in no prime disjoint from $S$. If $a \notin \hat S$, then $a/1$ is not a unit of $S^{-1}A$, so it lies in a maximal ideal of $S^{-1}A$, and by the prime correspondence of the next section the preimage of that ideal in $A$ is a prime disjoint from $S$ that contains $a$. For $S = \{f^n\}$ the primes disjoint from $S$ are those not containing $f$.

Algebraists localise at a prime $\mathfrak p$ (inverting its complement) but speak of inverting $p$ as localising away from $p$; category theorists localise at the morphisms to be inverted, which clashes with the first usage. The nForum thread on renaming nLab pages ended without consensus.

Grothendieck (EGA I, §1.3) says that $R[1/f]$ and $R[1/g]$ are canonically identified when $D(f) = D(g)$ and then treats them as equal; Buzzard reads this as a canonical isomorphism written as an equality. In a proof assistant the two are different types; Buzzard describes how a formalised lemma stated for the localisation $R[1/f]$ could not be applied to $R[1/f][1/g]$ until it was restated for any ring satisfying the characterisation above.

$R_{\mathfrak p}$ is the construction Localization.AtPrime p, built from the multiplicative set p.primeCompl $= R \setminus \mathfrak p$; $M_{\mathfrak p}$ is M.localizedModule p.primeCompl. Separately, the predicate IsLocalization.AtPrime S p says that a given $R$-algebra $S$ is a localisation of $R$ at $\mathfrak p$; Guan and Hu state results such as their Corollary 4.8 for any ring carrying this predicate, so that they apply to every model of $R_{\mathfrak p}$, in line with the characterisation by conditions (i)-(iii) above.

blocks.body:
- $A_{fg}$ and $(A_f)_g$ are canonically isomorphic, not literally equal. On paper this is harmless, but any argument that silently identifies two models must make sure the identifications are compatible; Buzzard's account of the Lean formalisation of schemes is a case where this mattered.
- "Localisation at $\mathfrak p$" inverts the elements outside $\mathfrak p$. "Localisation at $f$" inverts $f$. The same word does opposite things; read $A_{\mathfrak p}$ versus $A_f$ by whether the subscript is an ideal or an element.
- $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, $\mathbb Z[1/p]$, the $p$-adic integers and $\mathbb Z/p$ are four different rings.

blocks.title: Two stages for the integers
blocks.body: Show directly that $\mathbb Z[1/2][1/3] = \mathbb Z[1/6]$ inside $\mathbb Q$, and that $(\mathbb Z_{(5)})_{(0)} = \mathbb Q$.
blocks.solution: $\mathbb Z[1/2][1/3]$ consists of the $a/(2^m3^n)$. Since $1/2 = 3/6$ and $1/3 = 2/6$, both $1/2$ and $1/3$ lie in $\mathbb Z[1/6]$, so the left side is contained in $\mathbb Z[1/6]$; conversely $1/6 = (1/2)(1/3)$. For the second, $(0)\mathbb Z_{(5)}$ is the zero ideal of the domain $\mathbb Z_{(5)}$, and localising a domain at its zero prime gives its fraction field, which is $\mathbb Q$; this is the case $\mathfrak q = (0) \subseteq \mathfrak p = (5)$ of localisation in stages.

blocks.body:
1. (Basic) Use the universal property to construct, for every ring map $g\colon A \to B$ and multiplicative $S \subseteq A$, a ring map $S^{-1}A \to g(S)^{-1}B$, and show it is unique.
2. (Basic) Show that $\mathbb Z[x]/(2x - 1) \cong \mathbb Z[1/2]$ by exhibiting the map explicitly.
3. (Medium) Prove directly from Strickland's characterisation that $\mathbb Z/12 \to \mathbb Z/3$ is a localisation of $\mathbb Z/12$ at $\{1, 2, 4, 8\}$.
4. (Medium) Show that $\hat S$ is multiplicative and saturated, and that $S^{-1}A \to \hat S^{-1}A$ is an isomorphism.
5. (Harder) Show that $\mathbb Z[1/6]$ is not of the form $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ for any prime $p$, and that $\mathbb Z_{(2)}$ is not of the form $S^{-1}\mathbb Z$ for any finitely generated multiplicative set $S$.

blocks.title: Ideals and prime ideals of a localisation
blocks.body: For a ring map $\iota\colon A \to B$ there are two ways to move ideals. An ideal $I \subseteq A$ extends to $I^e = I B$, the ideal generated by $\iota(I)$; an ideal $J \subseteq B$ contracts to $J^c = \iota^{-1}(J)$. For a quotient map $A \to A/I$ these give the familiar correspondence theorem from [[rings]]. For localisation the behaviour is almost as good, and it is the reason localisation is so useful for studying primes: the prime ideals of $S^{-1}A$ are exactly the primes of $A$ that avoid $S$, and $S^{-1}A$ has no other ideals than extended ones. Gathmann proves the correspondence with the same ingredients as the Stacks Project and Sutherland; the Math 210B handout adds the explicit formula for $I^{ec}$ and the behaviour of primary ideals.

blocks.title: Extension and contraction for $S^{-1}A$
blocks.body:
Let $S \subseteq A$ be multiplicative and $\iota\colon A \to S^{-1}A$.

1. For an ideal $I \subseteq A$, $I^e = S^{-1}I = \{a/s : a \in I,\ s \in S\}$.
2. Every ideal $J$ of $S^{-1}A$ is extended: $J = (J^c)^e$.
3. $I^e = S^{-1}A$ if and only if $I \cap S \ne \varnothing$.
4. $I^{ec} = \{a \in A : sa \in I \text{ for some } s \in S\}$.
5. The maps $\mathfrak p \mapsto \mathfrak p^e$ and $\mathfrak q \mapsto \mathfrak q^c$ are mutually inverse, inclusion-preserving bijections between the primes of $A$ disjoint from $S$ and the primes of $S^{-1}A$. The same holds for primary ideals disjoint from $S$.
6. Extension commutes with sums, products, finite intersections and radicals: $(I + J)^e = I^e + J^e$, $(IJ)^e = I^eJ^e$, $(I \cap J)^e = I^e \cap J^e$, $(\sqrt I)^e = \sqrt{I^e}$.

1. The ideal generated by the $a/1$, $a \in I$, consists of sums $\sum (b_i/s_i)(a_i/1)$; bringing them to a common denominator gives a single fraction $a/s$ with $a \in I$. Conversely $a/s = (1/s)(a/1)$.

2. Let $J \subseteq S^{-1}A$. If $a/s \in J$ then $a/1 = (s/1)(a/s) \in J$, so $a \in J^c$ and $a/s \in (J^c)^e$. The reverse inclusion $(J^c)^e \subseteq J$ holds for every ring map.

3. If $s \in I \cap S$ then $1 = s/s \in I^e$. Conversely, if $1/1 = a/s$ with $a \in I$, then $u(s - a) = 0$ for some $u \in S$, so $us = ua \in I \cap S$.

4. If $b/1 = a/s$ with $a \in I$, then $u(bs - a) = 0$, so $(us)b = ua \in I$ with $us \in S$. Conversely, if $sb \in I$ then $b/1 = (sb)/s \in I^e$.

5. Let $\mathfrak q$ be a prime of $S^{-1}A$. Then $\mathfrak q^c$ is prime (contractions of primes are always prime) and disjoint from $S$, since $s \in \mathfrak q^c$ would make the unit $s/1$ lie in $\mathfrak q$. By (2), $\mathfrak q^{ce} = \mathfrak q$. Now let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime of $A$ with $\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing$. By (3), $\mathfrak p^e$ is proper. It is prime: if $(a/s)(b/t) \in \mathfrak p^e$, then $ab/st = c/r$ with $c \in \mathfrak p$, so $u(abr - cst) = 0$ and $uabr \in \mathfrak p$; as $u, r \notin \mathfrak p$, we get $ab \in \mathfrak p$, so $a$ or $b$ lies in $\mathfrak p$. By (4), $\mathfrak p^{ec} = \{a : sa \in \mathfrak p\} = \mathfrak p$, again because $s \notin \mathfrak p$. For a primary ideal $\mathfrak q_0$ with $\sqrt{\mathfrak q_0} \cap S = \varnothing$ the same two computations work, using that $sa \in \mathfrak q_0$ with $s \notin \sqrt{\mathfrak q_0}$ forces $a \in \mathfrak q_0$.

6. Sums and products: the generators of both sides agree. Intersections: $\subseteq$ is clear; if $x = a/s = b/t$ with $a \in I$, $b \in J$, then $u(at - bs) = 0$, and $c = uta = usb \in I \cap J$, so $x = c/(ust) \in (I \cap J)^e$. Radicals: if $(a/s)^n \in I^e$ then $a^n/s^n = b/t$ with $b \in I$, so $u(ta^n - s^nb) = 0$ and $(uta)^n \in I$ (multiply by $(ut)^{n-1}$); so $uta \in \sqrt I$ and $a/s = (uta)/(uts) \in (\sqrt I)^e$. The reverse inclusion is clear.

blocks.title: The local ring at a prime
blocks.body:
Let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime of $A$.

1. The primes of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ correspond to the primes of $A$ contained in $\mathfrak p$.
2. $A_{\mathfrak p}$ has exactly one maximal ideal, $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p} = \{a/s : a \in \mathfrak p,\ s \notin \mathfrak p\}$, and every element outside it is a unit.
3. The residue field is $A_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p} \cong \operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak p)$, written $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$.
4. $\dim A_{\mathfrak p} = \operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p$, the supremum of the lengths of chains of primes ending at $\mathfrak p$.

A ring with exactly one maximal ideal is called a local ring; local rings in general are the subject of [[local-rings]].

1. A prime is disjoint from $A \setminus \mathfrak p$ exactly when it is contained in $\mathfrak p$; apply part 5 of the previous theorem.

2. $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ is a proper ideal, by part 3 of the previous theorem. If $a/s \notin \mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ then $a \notin \mathfrak p$, so $s/a \in A_{\mathfrak p}$ is an inverse. Thus every proper ideal, consisting of non-units, lies inside $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$, which is therefore the unique maximal ideal.

3. Localisation commutes with quotients (Stacks, Proposition 10.9.14): $S^{-1}A/S^{-1}I \cong \bar S^{-1}(A/I)$, where $\bar S$ is the image of $S$ in $A/I$. With $S = A\setminus\mathfrak p$ and $I = \mathfrak p$, the image $\bar S$ is the set of all nonzero elements of the domain $A/\mathfrak p$, so $\bar S^{-1}(A/\mathfrak p) = \operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak p)$. (The isomorphism sends $\overline{a/s}$ to $\bar a/\bar s$; both maps are defined by the universal property.)

4. The bijection in (1) preserves inclusions, so chains of primes in $A_{\mathfrak p}$ are exactly chains of primes of $A$ inside $\mathfrak p$, and every such chain can be extended to end at $\mathfrak p$.

blocks.title: Spectra of localisations
blocks.body:
Write $\operatorname{Spec} A$ for the set of primes of $A$ with the Zariski topology, $V(I) = \{\mathfrak p \supseteq I\}$ closed and $D(f) = \{\mathfrak p : f \notin \mathfrak p\}$ open. Then:

1. $\operatorname{Spec} S^{-1}A \to \operatorname{Spec} A$, $\mathfrak q \mapsto \mathfrak q^c$, is a homeomorphism onto $\{\mathfrak p : \mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing\}$ with the subspace topology.
2. In particular $\operatorname{Spec} A_f \cong D(f)$, and $\operatorname{Spec} A_{\mathfrak p}$ is the set of primes contained in $\mathfrak p$.
3. $D(f) \cap D(g) = D(fg)$; $D(f) = \varnothing$ if and only if $f$ is nilpotent; the sets $D(f)$ form a basis of the topology.

1. The map is the bijection of the previous theorem onto the primes avoiding $S$. It is continuous because preimages of closed sets are closed: the preimage of $V(I)$ is $V(I^e)$. It is closed onto its image: a closed set of $\operatorname{Spec} S^{-1}A$ is $V(J)$ with $J = (J^c)^e$, and a prime $\mathfrak q$ contains $J$ iff $\mathfrak q^c \supseteq J^c$ (apply extension and contraction, which are inverse on primes), so $V(J)$ maps onto $V(J^c) \cap \operatorname{image}$.

2. For $S = \{f^n\}$, a prime avoids $S$ iff it does not contain $f$ (primes contain $f^n$ iff they contain $f$).

3. A prime contains $fg$ iff it contains $f$ or $g$. $D(f) = \varnothing$ means $f$ lies in every prime, i.e. in the nilradical (the intersection of all primes, see [[noetherian-rings]] and Stacks Lemma 10.17.2), i.e. $f$ is nilpotent; this matches $A_f = 0$ from the first section, as it must since $\operatorname{Spec} A_f = \varnothing$ iff $A_f = 0$. The complement of $V(I)$ is $\bigcup_{f \in I} D(f)$, so the $D(f)$ form a basis.

blocks.caption: The spectrum of $\mathbb Z$: one closed point $(p)$ for each prime and the generic point $(0)$, whose closure is the whole space because it is contained in every prime. Localising at the prime $(3)$ keeps the primes inside $(3)$, namely $(0)$ and $(3)$ (boxed); inverting $3$ keeps exactly the primes not containing $3$, everything except $(3)$ (crossed out).

Blue boxes enclose (3) and (0), labelled Spec of Z localized at 3 equals the two points (0) and (3). The point (3) is crossed out in red, and a red label says Spec Z[1/3] = D(3) consists of all points except (3).

blocks.title: Finiteness passes to localisations
blocks.body: If $A$ is Noetherian, so is every $S^{-1}A$. If $A$ is a principal ideal domain, so is every $S^{-1}A$ with $0 \notin S$. More precisely, if $a_1, \dots, a_n$ generate $I$, then $a_1/1, \dots, a_n/1$ generate $I^e$.

The generators of $I$ generate $I^e$ by part 1 of the extension theorem. Every ideal of $S^{-1}A$ is extended (part 2), so it is generated by the images of generators of an ideal of $A$: finitely many if $A$ is Noetherian, one if $A$ is a PID. A localisation of a domain at a set not containing $0$ is a subring of the fraction field, hence a domain.

blocks.title: What localisation preserves
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a domain and $S$ multiplicative with $0 \notin S$.

1. If $A$ is Noetherian, so is $S^{-1}A$; and $\dim S^{-1}A \le \dim A$.
2. Integral closure commutes with localisation: if $A \to B$ is a ring map and $B'$ is the integral closure of $A$ in $B$, then the integral closure of $S^{-1}A$ in $S^{-1}B$ is $S^{-1}B'$. In particular, if $A$ is integrally closed, so is $S^{-1}A$.
3. If $A$ is a Dedekind domain (Noetherian, integrally closed, every nonzero prime maximal), so is $S^{-1}A$.

1. Noetherian: this is the theorem 'Finiteness passes to localisations' above. Dimension: chains of primes in $S^{-1}A$ correspond to chains of primes of $A$ avoiding $S$.

2. (Stacks Lemma 10.36.11.) Elements of $S^{-1}B'$ are integral over $S^{-1}A$: if $b$ satisfies a monic equation over $A$, then $b/s$ satisfies the equation obtained by dividing by $s^n$, monic over $S^{-1}A$. Conversely, let $b/t \in S^{-1}B$ satisfy
$$(b/t)^n + (a_1/s_1)(b/t)^{n-1} + \dots + a_n/s_n = 0 .$$
Put $s = s_1\cdots s_n$ and multiply by $(st)^n$: we get $(sb)^n + c_1(sb)^{n-1} + \dots + c_n = 0$ in $S^{-1}B$ with $c_i \in A$ (each $c_i$ is $a_i$ times a product of the $s_j$ and of powers of $t$). So some $u \in S$ kills the left side in $B$; multiplying by $u^n$ gives a monic equation for $usb$ over $A$ in $B$. Hence $usb \in B'$ and $b/t = usb/ust \in S^{-1}B'$. Sutherland gives the same clearing-of-denominators argument for $B = \operatorname{Frac}(A)$, which is the second sentence.

3. Noetherian and integrally closed by 1 and 2. A nonzero prime of $S^{-1}A$ is $\mathfrak p^e$ with $\mathfrak p \ne 0$, so $\mathfrak p$ is maximal in $A$; any prime of $S^{-1}A$ containing $\mathfrak p^e$ contracts to a prime containing $\mathfrak p$, hence to $\mathfrak p$, so $\mathfrak p^e$ is maximal.

blocks.title: Primes of some localisations
blocks.body: Describe $\operatorname{Spec}$ of: (a) $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$; (b) $\mathbb Z[1/6]$; (c) $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ for a field $k$ (just say which primes of $k[x,y]$ survive); (d) $(\mathbb Z/12)_{(2)}$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Primes of $\mathbb Z$ inside $(p)$: $(0)$ and $(p)$. So $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ has exactly two primes, $0$ and the maximal ideal $p\mathbb Z_{(p)}$; its dimension is $1 = \operatorname{ht}(p)$.

(b) Primes of $\mathbb Z$ not containing $6$: $(0)$ and $(p)$ for $p \ne 2, 3$. This is the open set $D(6) = D(2) \cap D(3)$.

(c) The primes of $k[x,y]$ contained in $(x,y)$: the zero ideal, the maximal ideal $(x,y)$ itself, and the height one primes $(f)$ with $f$ irreducible and $f(0,0) = 0$ (curves through the origin). Geometrically, $k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ remembers the origin and every irreducible curve passing through it, and forgets everything else. Its dimension is $2 = \operatorname{ht}(x,y)$.

(d) The primes of $\mathbb Z/12$ are $(2)$ and $(3)$, and only $(2)$ is contained in $(2)$. So $(\mathbb Z/12)_{(2)}$ has a single prime. Here $S = \{1, 5, 7, 11\} \cup \{3, 9\}$, the elements outside $(2)$; inverting $3$ kills $\mathbb Z/3$ in $\mathbb Z/4 \times \mathbb Z/3$, and $(\mathbb Z/12)_{(2)} \cong \mathbb Z/4$, a local ring with maximal ideal $(2)$.

blocks.title: Localisation of a primary decomposition
blocks.body:
Let $I = \mathfrak q_1 \cap \dots \cap \mathfrak q_r$ be a primary decomposition with $\sqrt{\mathfrak q_i} = \mathfrak p_i$, and let $S$ be multiplicative. Number the components so that $\mathfrak p_1, \dots, \mathfrak p_m$ are disjoint from $S$ and $\mathfrak p_{m+1}, \dots, \mathfrak p_r$ meet $S$. Then
$$\begin{gathered}S^{-1}I = S^{-1}\mathfrak q_1 \cap \dots \cap S^{-1}\mathfrak q_m,\\ I^{ec} = \mathfrak q_1 \cap \dots \cap \mathfrak q_m,\end{gathered}$$
and these are primary decompositions. In words: localising throws away exactly the components that meet $S$.

Extension commutes with finite intersections, so $S^{-1}I = \bigcap_i S^{-1}\mathfrak q_i$. If $\mathfrak p_i$ meets $S$, so does $\mathfrak q_i$ (some power of an element of $\mathfrak p_i \cap S$ lies in $\mathfrak q_i$, and lies in $S$), and $S^{-1}\mathfrak q_i$ is the unit ideal. The other $S^{-1}\mathfrak q_i$ are primary with radical $S^{-1}\mathfrak p_i$ by part 5 of the extension theorem. Contracting, and using $\mathfrak q_i^{ec} = \mathfrak q_i$ for $i \le m$ together with the fact that contraction commutes with intersections, gives the second formula.

blocks.title: An embedded component disappears
blocks.body: In $A = k[x,y]$ let $I = (x^2, xy) = (x) \cap (x^2, y)$. Compute $I A_{(x)}$ and $I A_{(x,y)}$.
blocks.solution:
The components are $\mathfrak q_1 = (x)$, prime, and $\mathfrak q_2 = (x^2, y)$, primary with radical $(x, y)$. (Check of the decomposition: $I$ is contained in both. Conversely let $f = xg \in (x) \cap (x^2, y)$ and write $g = c + xg_1 + yg_2$ with $c \in k$; then $f \equiv cx$ modulo $I$, and since $I \subseteq (x^2, y)$, also $cx \in (x^2, y)$; setting $y = 0$ shows $c = 0$, so $f \in I$.)

At $\mathfrak p = (x)$: the radical $(x, y)$ is not contained in $(x)$, so it meets $A \setminus (x)$ (it contains $y$). The second component disappears, and $IA_{(x)} = xA_{(x)}$. Directly: $y$ is a unit in $A_{(x)}$, so $x = (xy)/y \in IA_{(x)}$.

At $\mathfrak m = (x, y)$: both radicals lie in $\mathfrak m$, nothing disappears, and $IA_{\mathfrak m} = xA_{\mathfrak m} \cap (x^2, y)A_{\mathfrak m}$ is strictly smaller than $xA_{\mathfrak m}$. Indeed $x/1 \notin IA_{\mathfrak m}$: by part 4 of the extension theorem this would need $sx \in I$ for some $s \notin \mathfrak m$, but $sx \in (x^2, xy)$ forces $s \in (x, y)$. Geometrically, the embedded point at the origin is invisible from the generic point of the line $x = 0$ but visible at the origin.

blocks.title: Heights, quotients and polynomial rings inside a localisation
blocks.body:
Guan and Hu's proof that $\operatorname{ht} I + \dim R/I = \dim R$ for Cohen-Macaulay local rings (their Theorem 4.19), and their proof that $R[X]$ is Cohen-Macaulay when $R$ is (their §4.2), pass between rings using three identifications. Prove them. Let $\mathfrak q \subseteq \mathfrak p$ be primes of $A$.

(a) $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}) = \operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q$.

(b) $A_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p} \cong (A/\mathfrak q)_{\mathfrak p/\mathfrak q}$; hence $\dim A_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p} = \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p/\mathfrak q)$, the length of the longest chain of primes from $\mathfrak q$ to $\mathfrak p$.

(c) If $P$ is a prime of $A[X]$ and $\mathfrak q = P \cap A$, then $A[X]_P \cong (A_{\mathfrak q}[X])_{PA_{\mathfrak q}[X]}$.
blocks.solution:
(a) By the theorem on the local ring at a prime, $\mathfrak q' \mapsto \mathfrak q'A_{\mathfrak p}$ is an inclusion-preserving bijection from the primes of $A$ inside $\mathfrak p$ to the primes of $A_{\mathfrak p}$, with inverse given by contraction. Every prime contained in $\mathfrak q$ lies inside $\mathfrak p$, so chains of primes of $A$ ending at $\mathfrak q$ correspond exactly to chains of primes of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ ending at $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}$, with the same lengths.

(b) The composite $A 	o A/\mathfrak q 	o (A/\mathfrak q)_{\mathfrak p/\mathfrak q}$ sends each $s 
otin \mathfrak p$ to a unit, since $ ar s 
otin \mathfrak p/\mathfrak q$. By the universal property it factors through $\psi\colon A_{\mathfrak p} 	o (A/\mathfrak q)_{\mathfrak p/\mathfrak q}$, $a/s \mapsto  ar a/ ar s$, which is surjective because every element of $(A/\mathfrak q) \setminus (\mathfrak p/\mathfrak q)$ is some $ ar s$ with $s 
otin \mathfrak p$. If $ ar a/ ar s = 0$, then $ ar u ar a = 0$ for some $u 
otin \mathfrak p$, i.e. $ua \in \mathfrak q$; as $u 
otin \mathfrak q$ (because $\mathfrak q \subseteq \mathfrak p$) and $\mathfrak q$ is prime, $a \in \mathfrak q$. Conversely $\psi$ kills $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}$. So $\ker\psi = \mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}$. The dimension statement is part 4 of the theorem on the local ring at a prime, applied to the prime $\mathfrak p/\mathfrak q$ of $A/\mathfrak q$, whose primes are the $\mathfrak q'/\mathfrak q$ with $\mathfrak q' \supseteq \mathfrak q$.

(c) Put $S = A \setminus \mathfrak q$ and $T = A[X] \setminus P$. Since $P \cap A = \mathfrak q$, $S \subseteq T$, so the products $st$ again lie in $T$ and $ST = T$. Localisation in stages gives $A[X]_P = T^{-1}A[X] \cong  ar T^{-1}(S^{-1}A[X])$. Next, $S^{-1}(A[X]) \cong A_{\mathfrak q}[X]$: the map $A[X] 	o A_{\mathfrak q}[X]$ inverts $S$, so it induces $\varphi\colon f/s \mapsto \sum_i (a_i/s)X^i$ for $f = \sum_i a_iX^i$. It is surjective (bring the coefficients to a common denominator), and injective: if all $a_i/s = 0$, there are $u_i \in S$ with $u_ia_i = 0$, and $u = \prod_i u_i$ satisfies $uf = 0$, so $f/s = 0$. Under $\varphi$, $S^{-1}P$ becomes $PA_{\mathfrak q}[X]$, a prime by the correspondence theorem since $P \cap S = \varnothing$. Finally, inverting $ ar T$ is the same as inverting the complement of $S^{-1}P$: an element $f/s$ lies outside $S^{-1}P$ exactly when $f \in T$, and then $f/s = (f/1)(1/s)$ with $1/s$ a unit, so both sets of elements become units in the same $S^{-1}A[X]$-algebras, and the universal property identifies the two localisations. Hence $A[X]_P \cong (A_{\mathfrak q}[X])_{PA_{\mathfrak q}[X]}$, which is the form in which Guan and Hu use it.

blocks.body:
- The correspondence is a bijection on primes, not on all ideals. Every ideal of $S^{-1}A$ is extended, but different ideals of $A$ can extend to the same one: in $\mathbb Z_{(2)}$ the ideals $(2)$, $(6)$ and $(10)$ all extend to $2\mathbb Z_{(2)}$, because $3$ and $5$ become units. Only the ideals with $I = I^{ec}$, those that are "$S$-saturated", are recovered.
- A general localisation is not a local ring. $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ has infinitely many maximal ideals; only localisations at the complement of a prime are guaranteed to be local. Chevalley already remarks that if one inverts only the non-zero-divisors outside a prime $\mathfrak u$, the resulting ring in general fails to be local.
- An element written $a/s$ with $s \in \mathfrak p$ may still lie in $A_{\mathfrak p}$ ($9/3 = 3/1$ in $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$); what matters is whether some representative has denominator outside $\mathfrak p$.

1. (Basic) List the primes of $\mathbb Z[1/10]$ and of $\mathbb Z_{(5)}$. Which of them are maximal?
2. (Basic) In $\mathbb Z_{(2)}$, show that every nonzero ideal is $2^k\mathbb Z_{(2)}$ for a unique $k \ge 0$.
3. (Medium) Let $A = k[x,y]$ and $\mathfrak p = (y)$. Show that $A_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p} \cong k(x)$, the field of rational functions in $x$.
4. (Medium) Show that $S^{-1}(\sqrt{0}) = \sqrt{0}$ in $S^{-1}A$: the nilradical commutes with localisation.
5. (Harder) Let $I \subseteq A$ and $S$ multiplicative. Show that the primes of $S^{-1}A$ containing $S^{-1}I$ correspond to the primes of $A$ containing $I$ and disjoint from $S$, and deduce $\operatorname{Spec}((A/I)_{\bar f}) \cong V(I) \cap D(f)$.

blocks.title: Localising modules
blocks.body: The same fractions make sense with numerators in a module. Localising modules is what makes localisation a tool rather than a curiosity: it turns an $A$-module into an $S^{-1}A$-module, it preserves exact sequences, and it agrees with base change along $A \to S^{-1}A$. The results in this section are used in every paper in our list, usually without being stated.

blocks.title: Localisation of a module
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be an $A$-module and $S \subseteq A$ multiplicative. On $M \times S$ put $(m, s) \sim (n, t)$ iff $u(tm - sn) = 0$ for some $u \in S$, and let $S^{-1}M$ be the set of classes $m/s$. With
$$\frac{m}{s} + \frac{n}{t} = \frac{tm + sn}{st}, \qquad \frac{a}{s}\cdot\frac{m}{t} = \frac{am}{st},$$
$S^{-1}M$ is an $S^{-1}A$-module, and $m \mapsto m/1$ is $A$-linear. One writes $M_f$ and $M_{\mathfrak p}$ as for rings. An $A$-linear map $\varphi\colon M \to N$ induces the $S^{-1}A$-linear map $S^{-1}\varphi\colon m/s \mapsto \varphi(m)/s$, and $S^{-1}$ is a functor. The checks that $\sim$ is an equivalence and the operations are well defined are word for word those for rings.

blocks.title: Localisation is exact
blocks.body:
If $L \xrightarrow{\alpha} M \xrightarrow{\beta} N$ is exact, then $S^{-1}L \to S^{-1}M \to S^{-1}N$ is exact. Consequently localisation preserves injections, surjections, kernels, images and cokernels, and for submodules $N, N' \subseteq M$:
$$\begin{aligned}S^{-1}(M/N) &\cong S^{-1}M/S^{-1}N,\\ S^{-1}(N + N') &= S^{-1}N + S^{-1}N',\\ S^{-1}(N \cap N') &= S^{-1}N \cap S^{-1}N',\\ S^{-1}(M \oplus M') &\cong S^{-1}M \oplus S^{-1}M'.\end{aligned}$$

The composite $S^{-1}\beta \circ S^{-1}\alpha = S^{-1}(\beta\alpha) = 0$. Conversely let $m/s \in \ker S^{-1}\beta$, i.e. $\beta(m)/s = 0$, so $u\beta(m) = 0$ for some $u \in S$. Then $um \in \ker\beta = \operatorname{im}\alpha$, say $um = \alpha(l)$, and $m/s = um/us = S^{-1}\alpha(l/us)$.

For the consequences: apply exactness to $0 \to N \to M \to M/N \to 0$ to get the quotient formula, and to $0 \to \ker \to M \to N$, $M \to N \to \operatorname{coker} \to 0$ for kernels and cokernels. Sums: $S^{-1}(N + N')$ is the image of $S^{-1}(N \oplus N')$, and direct sums are preserved because a fraction $(n, n')/s$ is the same as $(n/s, n'/s)$. Intersections: $N \cap N'$ is the kernel of $M \to M/N \oplus M/N'$, and kernels and finite direct sums are preserved.

blocks.title: Localisation is base change
blocks.body:
For every $A$-module $M$ there is an isomorphism of $S^{-1}A$-modules
$$\begin{gathered}S^{-1}A \otimes_A M \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } S^{-1}M,\\ \frac{a}{s} \otimes m \mapsto \frac{am}{s},\end{gathered}$$
natural in $M$. Consequently $S^{-1}A$ is a flat $A$-module: $S^{-1}A \otimes_A -$ preserves injective maps.

We use the tensor product of $A$-modules as in [[tensor-products]]: $P \otimes_A M$ is generated by symbols $p \otimes m$, bilinear in $p$ and $m$, with $ap \otimes m = p \otimes am$, and a map out of it is the same as an $A$-bilinear map out of $P \times M$.

The map $(a/s, m) \mapsto am/s$ is well defined (if $a/s = b/t$ with $u(at - bs) = 0$, then $u(t\cdot am - s\cdot bm) = 0$) and bilinear, so it induces $\Phi\colon S^{-1}A \otimes_A M \to S^{-1}M$, which is surjective since $m/s = \Phi((1/s) \otimes m)$.

Every element of the tensor product has the form $(1/s) \otimes m$: given $\sum_i (a_i/s_i) \otimes m_i$, put $s = \prod s_i$ and $s_i' = s/s_i$; then $(a_i/s_i) \otimes m_i = (a_is_i'/s) \otimes m_i$, which equals $(1/s) \otimes a_is_i'm_i$, and the sum is $(1/s) \otimes \sum_i a_is_i'm_i$.

Injectivity: suppose $\Phi((1/s) \otimes m) = m/s = 0$, i.e. $um = 0$ for some $u \in S$. Then $(1/s) \otimes m = (u/us) \otimes m = (1/us) \otimes um = 0$.

Flatness: if $N \to M$ is injective then so is $S^{-1}N \to S^{-1}M$, by exactness, and under the isomorphism this is $S^{-1}A \otimes N \to S^{-1}A \otimes M$.

items.label: Fractions
items.body: Classes $m/s$ under $u(tm - sn) = 0$: the definition in the Stacks Project and Gathmann, convenient for computing kernels.

items.label: Base change
items.body: $S^{-1}M = S^{-1}A \otimes_A M$, so module localisation is extension of scalars along $A \to S^{-1}A$. Gathmann proves it as Lemma 6.19; Vakil marks the isomorphism as an important exercise (2.3.K) and uses it to transport facts about tensor products.

items.label: Reflection
items.body: $S^{-1}A$-modules are the same as $A$-modules on which every $s \in S$ acts bijectively (Stacks Lemma 10.9.5), and $M \to S^{-1}M$ is the universal map from $M$ to such a module: for any $N$ on which $S$ acts invertibly, $\operatorname{Hom}_A(S^{-1}M, N) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_A(M, N)$ (Lemma 10.9.7). In Vakil's terms (Exercise 2.5.G) localisation is left adjoint to the forgetful functor from $S^{-1}A$-modules to $A$-modules.

items.label: Colimit
items.body: $S^{-1}M = \operatorname{colim}_{f \in S} M_f$, the colimit over $S$ preordered by divisibility (Stacks Lemma 10.9.9; Vakil Exercise 2.4.E for rings). So a general localisation is built from localisations at single elements, which is how the stalk $\mathcal O_{X,\mathfrak p} = A_{\mathfrak p}$ arises from the rings $A_f$ with $f \notin \mathfrak p$.

blocks.title: Localising a finitely generated abelian group
blocks.body: Let $M = \mathbb Z \oplus \mathbb Z/4 \oplus \mathbb Z/9 \oplus \mathbb Z/5$. Compute $M_{(2)}$, $M_{(3)}$, $M[1/2]$ and $M \otimes_{\mathbb Z} \mathbb Q$.
blocks.solution:
Localisation commutes with finite direct sums, so localise each summand. For a cyclic module, $S^{-1}(\mathbb Z/n) = S^{-1}\mathbb Z/nS^{-1}\mathbb Z$ by the quotient formula.

At $(2)$: $\mathbb Z_{(2)}/4\mathbb Z_{(2)} \cong \mathbb Z/4$, while $9$ and $5$ are units of $\mathbb Z_{(2)}$, so $\mathbb Z_{(2)}/9\mathbb Z_{(2)} = 0 = \mathbb Z_{(2)}/5\mathbb Z_{(2)}$. Thus $M_{(2)} \cong \mathbb Z_{(2)} \oplus \mathbb Z/4$.

At $(3)$: $M_{(3)} \cong \mathbb Z_{(3)} \oplus \mathbb Z/9$.

Inverting $2$: $4$ becomes a unit, killing $\mathbb Z/4$; the others survive because $9$ and $5$ stay non-units and $\mathbb Z[1/2]/9\mathbb Z[1/2] \cong \mathbb Z/9$ ($2$ is already invertible mod $9$). So $M[1/2] \cong \mathbb Z[1/2] \oplus \mathbb Z/9 \oplus \mathbb Z/5$.

Over $\mathbb Q$ every nonzero integer is a unit: $M \otimes \mathbb Q \cong \mathbb Q$. The torsion is invisible, and the rank of $M$ is $\dim_{\mathbb Q} M \otimes \mathbb Q = 1$. In terms of the structure theorem of [[modules]], localising at $(p)$ keeps the free part and the $p$-primary part and discards the rest.

blocks.title: Hom and localisation
blocks.body:
If $M$ is finitely presented (there is an exact sequence $A^m \to A^n \to M \to 0$), then for every $A$-module $N$ the natural map
$$\begin{aligned}&S^{-1}\operatorname{Hom}_A(M, N)\\ &\qquad\to \operatorname{Hom}_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M, S^{-1}N),\end{aligned}$$
given by $\varphi/s \mapsto (1/s)S^{-1}\varphi$, is an isomorphism. If $M$ is only finitely generated, it is injective, and two maps $M \to N$ agree after localising iff $s\varphi = s\psi$ for some $s \in S$.

Following the hint in Vakil's Exercise 2.6.G: $\operatorname{Hom}_A(-, N)$ is left exact, so the presentation gives an exact sequence $0 \to \operatorname{Hom}_A(M, N) \to N^n \to N^m$. Localising, which is exact, gives
$$\begin{aligned}0 \to S^{-1}\operatorname{Hom}_A(M, N) &\to (S^{-1}N)^n\\ &\to (S^{-1}N)^m .\end{aligned}$$
On the other hand the localised presentation $(S^{-1}A)^m \to (S^{-1}A)^n \to S^{-1}M \to 0$ is exact, and $\operatorname{Hom}_{S^{-1}A}(-, S^{-1}N)$ gives an exact sequence
$$\begin{aligned}0 \to \operatorname{Hom}(S^{-1}M, S^{-1}N) &\to (S^{-1}N)^n\\ &\to (S^{-1}N)^m\end{aligned}$$
with the same right-hand map (it is given by the same matrix). Both are kernels of the same map, and the natural map is compatible with the inclusions, so it is an isomorphism. For $M$ finitely generated only the first half of the argument is available ($A^n \to M \to 0$), which gives injectivity; this is Lombardi's Fait 1.13, and the finitely presented case is his Fait 1.14.

The finiteness hypothesis in Vakil's and Lombardi's statements cannot be dropped. Let $M = \bigoplus_p \mathbb Z/p$ over all primes $p$, and $S = \mathbb Z \setminus \{0\}$. Then $S^{-1}M = M \otimes \mathbb Q = 0$, so the right side is $0$; but $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(M, M) = \prod_p \mathbb Z/p$ contains the element $(1, 1, 1, \dots)$, which no nonzero integer kills, so $S^{-1}\operatorname{Hom}(M, M) \ne 0$.

blocks.title: Support of a module
blocks.body: The support of an $A$-module $M$ is $\operatorname{Supp} M = \{\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Spec} A : M_{\mathfrak p} \ne 0\}$, the set of points of $\operatorname{Spec} A$ at which $M$ does not vanish.

blocks.title: Support of a finitely generated module
blocks.body: If $M$ is finitely generated, $\operatorname{Supp} M = V(\operatorname{Ann} M)$, a closed subset of $\operatorname{Spec} A$ (Stacks Lemma 10.40.5).

If $\mathfrak p 
ot\supseteq \operatorname{Ann} M$, pick $s \in \operatorname{Ann} M \setminus \mathfrak p$; it kills every $m$, so $m/t = sm/st = 0$ and $M_{\mathfrak p} = 0$. Conversely, if $M_{\mathfrak p} = 0$ and $x_1, \dots, x_n$ generate $M$, then each $x_i/1 = 0$, so $s_ix_i = 0$ for some $s_i 
otin \mathfrak p$; the product $s = s_1\cdots s_n 
otin \mathfrak p$ kills all generators, so $s \in \operatorname{Ann} M \setminus \mathfrak p$.

1. (Basic) Compute $(\mathbb Z/12)_{(3)}$ and $(\mathbb Z/12)_{(5)}$ as $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$- and $\mathbb Z_{(5)}$-modules.
2. (Basic) Show that $S^{-1}(I) \cong I \otimes_A S^{-1}A \cong IS^{-1}A$ for an ideal $I$, i.e. tensoring an ideal with $S^{-1}A$ does not create torsion.
3. (Medium) Find $\operatorname{Supp}_{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ and show that it is not closed. Why does this not contradict the theorem above?
4. (Medium) Show that for $A$-modules $M, N$: $S^{-1}(M \otimes_A N) \cong S^{-1}M \otimes_{S^{-1}A} S^{-1}N$.
5. (Harder) Show that a module $M$ is flat if and only if $M_{\mathfrak m}$ is a flat $A_{\mathfrak m}$-module for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. (Use the local-global principle of the next section and the previous exercise.)

blocks.title: Local properties and the local-global principle
blocks.body: A property of rings or modules is local if it holds for $A$ (or $M$) exactly when it holds for every localisation $A_{\mathfrak p}$ (or $M_{\mathfrak p}$), equivalently for every $A_{\mathfrak m}$ with $\mathfrak m$ maximal. Atiyah-Macdonald have a section called Local properties, Gathmann proves the basic cases in Proposition 6.27 and the exercises after it, and Lombardi gives "concrete" versions in which the infinitely many primes are replaced by finitely many elements generating the unit ideal. The second form is the one that glues: it is the algebra behind the structure sheaf of an affine scheme.

blocks.title: Basic local properties
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be an $A$-module. The following hold, and in each case "for all primes" may be replaced by "for all maximal ideals".

1. $M = 0$ if and only if $M_{\mathfrak p} = 0$ for all primes $\mathfrak p$.
2. A sequence $L \to M \to N$ is exact if and only if all $L_{\mathfrak p} \to M_{\mathfrak p} \to N_{\mathfrak p}$ are exact. In particular injectivity and surjectivity of a map are local.
3. For submodules $N, N' \subseteq M$: $N \subseteq N'$ iff $N_{\mathfrak p} \subseteq N'_{\mathfrak p}$ for all $\mathfrak p$; so equality of ideals is local.
4. $A$ is reduced iff every $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is reduced.
5. An element $x \in M$ is zero iff $x/1 = 0$ in every $M_{\mathfrak m}$.

5 (and hence 1). Suppose $x \ne 0$. Its annihilator $\operatorname{Ann}(x)$ is a proper ideal (it misses $1$), so it is contained in some maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. If $x/1 = 0$ in $M_{\mathfrak m}$ there is $s \notin \mathfrak m$ with $sx = 0$, i.e. $s \in \operatorname{Ann}(x) \subseteq \mathfrak m$, a contradiction. So some $x/1 \ne 0$. Applying this to every $x$ gives 1 for maximal ideals; the version with all primes follows since $M_{\mathfrak m} = 0$ is among the conditions.

2. One direction is exactness of localisation. Conversely let $H = \ker(M \to N)/\operatorname{im}(L \to M)$. Localisation commutes with kernels, images and quotients, so $H_{\mathfrak m}$ is the homology of the localised sequence, which is $0$. By 1, $H = 0$.

3. Apply 1 to $(N + N')/N'$, whose localisation is $(N_{\mathfrak p} + N'_{\mathfrak p})/N'_{\mathfrak p}$.

4. The nilradical commutes with localisation (exercise 4 of the section on ideals, or part 6 of the extension theorem applied to $I = 0$): $\sqrt{0}_{\mathfrak p} = \sqrt{0_{A_{\mathfrak p}}}$. By 1, $\sqrt 0 = 0$ iff all its localisations vanish.

blocks.title: A domain is the intersection of its localisations
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a domain with fraction field $K$. Inside $K$,
$$A = \bigcap_{\mathfrak m \text{ maximal}} A_{\mathfrak m} = \bigcap_{\mathfrak p \text{ prime}} A_{\mathfrak p}.$$
For example $\mathbb Z = \bigcap_p \mathbb Z_{(p)}$.

Clearly $A$ lies in every $A_{\mathfrak p}$, and $\bigcap_{\mathfrak p} \subseteq \bigcap_{\mathfrak m}$. Let $x \in K$ lie in every $A_{\mathfrak m}$ and consider the ideal of denominators $D = \{d \in A : dx \in A\}$. For each $\mathfrak m$ write $x = a/s$ with $s \notin \mathfrak m$; then $sx = a \in A$, so $s \in D \setminus \mathfrak m$. Thus $D$ is contained in no maximal ideal, so $D = A$, $1 \in D$, and $x \in A$. (Sutherland deduces the statement, also for ideals and modules, from his Proposition 2.6.)

blocks.title: Being a domain is not local
blocks.body: Let $A = \mathbb Z/6$. Show that every localisation of $A$ at a prime is a field, but $A$ is not a domain.
blocks.solution: $A \cong \mathbb Z/2 \times \mathbb Z/3$ has the two primes $\mathfrak p_2 = (2)$ and $\mathfrak p_3 = (3)$. At $\mathfrak p_2$, the element $3 \notin \mathfrak p_2$ becomes invertible, and $3 \cdot 2 = 0$, so $2/1 = 0$; hence $A_{\mathfrak p_2}$ is a quotient of $A/(2) = \mathbb F_2$, and it is nonzero (localising at a prime never gives $0$), so $A_{\mathfrak p_2} \cong \mathbb F_2$. Similarly $A_{\mathfrak p_3} \cong \mathbb F_3$. Both are fields, in particular domains, but $2 \cdot 3 = 0$ in $A$. Gathmann's Exercise 6.29 asks for exactly this phenomenon (being a domain is not a local property), and Wikipedia mentions a more drastic case: an infinite product of fields is neither a domain nor Noetherian, although all its local rings are fields. Geometrically, $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is two points, and a domain must have irreducible spectrum, a condition that cannot be seen one point at a time.

blocks.title: Concrete local-global principle

blocks.body:
First, for any $N \ge 1$ the powers $s_1^N, \dots, s_n^N$ also generate the unit ideal: from $1 = \sum c_is_i$, raising to the power $n(N-1) + 1$ and expanding, every monomial contains some $s_i$ with exponent at least $N$.

1. $m/1 = 0$ in $M_{s_i}$ means $s_i^{N_i}m = 0$. Take $N = \max N_i$ and write $1 = \sum d_is_i^N$; then $m = \sum d_is_i^Nm = 0$.

2. If $a/1$ is a unit in $A_{s_i}$ then $(a/1)(b_i/s_i^{k}) = 1$, so $s_i^{l}(ab_i - s_i^{k}) = 0$ and $s_i^{k+l} \in aA$. So the ideal $aA$ contains a power of each $s_i$, hence a set of elements generating the unit ideal (raise to a common exponent as above), so $aA = A$.

3. If $ab = 0$ then $(a/1)(b/1) = 0$ in each $A_{s_i}$, so $b/1 = 0$ in each $A_{s_i}$, and $b = 0$ by 1. The converse uses that $A \to A_{s_i}$ is flat: multiplication by $a$ is injective on $A$, hence on $A_{s_i}$ by exactness.

blocks.title: Glueing: the sheaf condition for localisations
blocks.body:
Let $f_1, \dots, f_n$ generate the unit ideal of $A$ and let $M$ be an $A$-module. Then the sequence
$$0 \to M \xrightarrow{\ \alpha\ } \bigoplus_{i} M_{f_i} \xrightarrow{\ \beta\ } \bigoplus_{i,j} M_{f_if_j}$$
is exact, where $\alpha(m) = (m/1)_i$ and $\beta\big((m_i)_i\big) = (m_i - m_j)_{i,j}$, the differences being taken in $M_{f_if_j}$ (into which both $M_{f_i}$ and $M_{f_j}$ map).

This is the Stacks Project's argument (Lemma 10.24.1). By the local properties above, exactness may be checked after localising at each maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. Localising at $\mathfrak m$ commutes with the finite direct sums and with the localisations $M_{f_i}$ (localisation in stages: both $(M_{f_i})_{\mathfrak m}$ and $(M_{\mathfrak m})_{f_i}$ invert the same multiplicative set). Since the $f_i$ generate the unit ideal, not all lie in $\mathfrak m$; renumber so that $f_1 \notin \mathfrak m$. After localising, $f_1$ is a unit, and we may assume $f_1 = 1$, so $M_{f_1} = M$ and $M_{f_1f_j} = M_{f_j}$.

Now $\alpha$ is injective, because its first component is the identity of $M$. If $(m_i) \in \ker\beta$, then in particular $m_1 - m_j = 0$ in $M_{f_1f_j} = M_{f_j}$ for every $j$, i.e. $m_j$ is the image of $m_1 \in M$. Thus $(m_i) = \alpha(m_1)$.

blocks.caption: The glueing sequence for $A = M = \mathbb Z$ and the generators $f_1 = 2$, $f_2 = 3$ of the unit ideal (keeping only the component $(1,2)$ of $\beta$, as the others are $0$ or determined by it), with $\beta(x, y) = x - y$. Exactness in the middle says $\mathbb Z[1/2] \cap \mathbb Z[1/3] = \mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb Z[1/6]$: a rational number whose denominator is both a power of $2$ and a power of $3$ is an integer.
blocks.alt: An exact sequence: 0, then Z, then the direct sum of Z[1/2] and Z[1/3], then Z[1/6], with arrows alpha and beta.

items.label: Algebraic
items.body: A property is local when it can be tested on all $A_{\mathfrak p}$, or all $A_{\mathfrak m}$; the proofs reduce to the fact that a module whose localisations vanish is zero.

items.label: Geometric
items.body: Localising at $f$ restricts to the open set $D(f)$, where $f$ does not vanish; localising at $\mathfrak p$ keeps only the germs of functions at the point $\mathfrak p$. The nLab phrases this through the duality between rings and spaces: $\operatorname{Spec} R[S^{-1}] \to \operatorname{Spec} R$ are the basic open immersions.

items.label: Constructive
items.body: Lombardi replaces "for every prime" by "on each $A[1/s_i]$ for finitely many comaximal $s_i$". The abstract principle (all primes) needs choice to produce primes; the concrete one does not, and Lombardi shows how proofs using the abstract version can be turned into algorithms that output the $s_i$.

items.label: Not very local
items.body: Grossack points out that Zariski open sets are dense, so the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ still remembers a lot of global information: for varieties over an algebraically closed field $k$, if the local rings at a point of $X$ and a point of $Y$ are isomorphic as $k$-algebras, the points have isomorphic open neighbourhoods, so $X$ and $Y$ are birational. To see a genuinely small neighbourhood one completes: by the Cohen structure theorem, regular points of varieties of the same dimension over $k$ all have completed local ring $k[\![x_1, \dots, x_n]\!]$, as in the manifold picture.

blocks.title: Global notions defined locally
blocks.body:
Many classes of rings are defined by a condition on all localisations, and a theorem then shows that maximal ideals suffice.

1. Regular rings: $A$ is regular if every $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a regular local ring (Guan-Hu Definition 5.18); it suffices to check maximal ideals (their Theorem 5.20).
2. Cohen-Macaulay rings: every $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a Cohen-Macaulay local ring (Definition 4.11); again maximal ideals suffice (Lemma 4.12).
3. Dedekind domains: a Noetherian domain all of whose localisations at nonzero primes are discrete valuation rings (Sutherland, Proposition 2.9 and Definition 2.10; see [[dedekind-domains]]).
4. Homological invariants: for a finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring, $\operatorname{pd} M = \sup_{\mathfrak p} \operatorname{pd} M_{\mathfrak p}$ and $\operatorname{gldim} A = \sup_{\mathfrak p} \operatorname{gldim} A_{\mathfrak p}$ (Guan-Hu Lemmas 2.9 and 2.14); localisation can only lower projective dimension (Lemma 2.10), because it carries projective resolutions to projective resolutions.
5. Projective modules: a finitely presented module is projective iff all its localisations are free; concretely (Lombardi) iff there are comaximal $s_i$ with each $M_{s_i}$ free.

The definitions of regular and Cohen-Macaulay local rings are not given here; see [[homological-algebra]] for the tools, and Guan-Hu for a complete formal treatment.

blocks.title: Localising at an idempotent
blocks.body: If $e \in A$ is idempotent ($e^2 = e$), then $A_e \cong A/(1 - e) \cong eA$, where $eA$ is a ring with identity $e$. If $e_1, \dots, e_n$ are orthogonal idempotents with $\sum e_i = 1$, then $A \cong A_{e_1} \times \dots \times A_{e_n}$, and similarly for modules.

The map $A \to A/(1-e)$ sends $e$ to $1$, a unit, so it factors through $A_e$; and in $A_e$ we have $e/1 \cdot (1 - e)/1 = 0$ with $e/1$ a unit, so $1 - e$ dies, giving the inverse map $A/(1-e) \to A_e$. The map $A \to eA$, $a \mapsto ea$, is a surjective ring map with kernel $(1 - e)A$ (if $ea = 0$ then $a = (1-e)a$). For orthogonal idempotents, $A \to \prod eA$, $a \mapsto (e_ia)_i$, is an isomorphism with inverse $(a_i) \mapsto \sum a_i$, which is Lombardi's Fait 1.17.

blocks.title: Glueing and idempotents in a small ring
blocks.body: (a) In $A = \mathbb Z/6$ find the idempotents and compute $A_e$ for each. (b) For the glueing sequence with $A = \mathbb Z$, $f_1 = 2$, $f_2 = 3$, take $x = 5/2 \in \mathbb Z[1/2]$ and $y = 7/3 \in \mathbb Z[1/3]$. Compute $\beta(x, y)$, decide whether $(x, y)$ lies in the image of $\alpha$, and describe all pairs in $\ker\beta$.
blocks.solution:
(a) $e^2 = e$ in $\mathbb Z/6$ means $6 \mid e(e-1)$: $e \in \{0, 1, 3, 4\}$. Then $A_0 = 0$, $A_1 = A$, $A_3 \cong A/(1 - 3) = A/(2) \cong \mathbb F_2$ and $A_4 \cong A/(1-4) = A/(3) \cong \mathbb F_3$. The orthogonal pair $3, 4$ (indeed $3\cdot 4 = 12 \equiv 0$ and $3 + 4 \equiv 1$) recovers $\mathbb Z/6 \cong \mathbb F_2 \times \mathbb F_3$. Inverting the idempotent $3$ gives the same ring as localising at the prime $(2)$, computed in the example on domains.

(b) $\beta(x, y) = 5/2 - 7/3 = 1/6 \ne 0$ in $\mathbb Z[1/6]$, so $(x, y) \notin \ker\beta = \operatorname{im}\alpha$. In general a pair $(x, y)$ with $x = y$ in $\mathbb Z[1/6]$ must have $x \in \mathbb Z[1/2] \cap \mathbb Z[1/3] = \mathbb Z$, and then $(x, y) = \alpha(x)$. The partition of unity behind the proof is $1 = (-1)\cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 3$.

1. (Basic) Show that an $A$-module map $\varphi\colon M \to N$ is an isomorphism iff every $\varphi_{\mathfrak m}$ is.
2. (Basic) Find comaximal $s_1, s_2 \in \mathbb Z$ such that $\mathbb Z[1/s_1]$ and $\mathbb Z[1/s_2]$ are both PIDs with $\mathbb Z = \mathbb Z[1/s_1] \cap \mathbb Z[1/s_2]$, and check the glueing sequence by hand.
3. (Medium) Show that $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is covered by finitely many $D(f_i)$ iff the $f_i$ generate the unit ideal, and deduce that $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is quasi-compact.
4. (Medium) Show that being Noetherian is not a local property, using an infinite product of fields $\prod_{\mathbb N} \mathbb F_2$: every localisation at a prime is a field. (You may use that every element $x$ of this ring is idempotent.)
5. (Harder) Prove the glueing theorem directly, without localising at maximal ideals: given elements $m_i/f_i^N \in M_{f_i}$ that agree in every $M_{f_if_j}$, use an equation $1 = \sum_i c_if_i^K$ for a suitable $K$ to write down $m \in M$ with $m/1 = m_i/f_i^N$ in each $M_{f_i}$.

blocks.title: Affine schemes in one paragraph
blocks.body:
The theorem on spectra of localisations and the glueing theorem above are why localisations are the local functions of algebraic geometry. On $X = \operatorname{Spec} A$ the open sets $D(f)$ form a basis, $D(f) \cap D(g) = D(fg)$, and $D(f) \subseteq D(g)$ gives a restriction map $A_g \to A_f$ (since $g$ is then invertible in $A_f$). Assigning $A_f$ to $D(f)$ defines a sheaf on this basis, because if $D(f) = \bigcup_i D(f_i)$ then the $f_i$ generate the unit ideal of $A_f$ and the glueing sequence for the ring $A_f$ is exactly the sheaf condition. The resulting sheaf $\mathcal O_X$ satisfies (Stacks Lemma 26.5.4; Vakil §5.1)
$$\begin{gathered}\Gamma(X, \mathcal O_X) = A,\qquad \Gamma(D(f), \mathcal O_X) = A_f,\\ \mathcal O_{X, \mathfrak p} = A_{\mathfrak p},\end{gathered}$$
the last because the stalk is the colimit of the $A_f$ over $f \notin \mathfrak p$, which is $A_{\mathfrak p}$ by the colimit description of localisation. Its stalks are local rings, so $(X, \mathcal O_X)$ is a locally ringed space (see [[local-rings]]), and a ring map $A \to B$ induces a morphism of locally ringed spaces $\operatorname{Spec} B \to \operatorname{Spec} A$ (the stalk maps $A_{\mathfrak q^c} \to B_{\mathfrak q}$ are local). Xu's paper reproduces these steps for commutative $\mathbb F_1$-algebras: the universal property of $S^{-1}A$ (his Theorem 3.5), then stalks $A_{\mathfrak p}$, sections $A_f$ over $D(f)$ and global sections $A$ (Theorem 5.4), with morphisms required to be local on stalks (Definition 5.5), and obtains an anti-equivalence between commutative $\mathbb F_1$-algebras and what he calls absolute affine schemes. The details belong to [[schemes]].

1. (Basic) Show that if $D(f) \subseteq D(g)$ then $g$ is a unit in $A_f$, so there is a unique map $A_g \to A_f$ under $A$.
2. (Basic) For $X = \operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ compute the stalks at $(0)$ and at $(p)$, and $\Gamma(D(6), \mathcal O_X)$.
3. (Basic) Let $D$ be a domain and $f, g \in D$ nonzero. Show that $D[1/f] \subseteq D[1/g]$ inside $\operatorname{Frac} D$ if and only if every prime of $D$ containing $f$ contains $g$. Compare with exercise 1.
4. (Medium) Show that if $D(f) = D(g)$ then $A_f$ and $A_g$ are canonically isomorphic under $A$, although they need not be equal as sets of fractions.
5. (Medium) Let $\varphi\colon A \to B$ be a ring map, $\mathfrak q$ a prime of $B$ and $\mathfrak p = \varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. Show that the induced map $A_{\mathfrak p} \to B_{\mathfrak q}$ is a local homomorphism (in the sense of [[local-rings]]).

Prerequisites: [[noetherian-rings]] and [[modules]], with [[tensor-products]] for the base-change description of $S^{-1}M$.

- [[local-rings]]: every $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a local ring; local rings in general, local homomorphisms, locally ringed spaces, Nakayama's lemma and the local rings of affine space at a point are treated there.
- [[schemes]]: the structure sheaf of $\operatorname{Spec} A$ is built from the rings $A_f$ on the basic open sets $D(f)$, with stalks $A_{\mathfrak p}$; schemes are locally ringed spaces glued from these.
- [[dedekind-domains]]: Dedekind domains are the Noetherian domains whose localisations at nonzero primes are discrete valuation rings; discrete valuation rings, class groups of localisations such as $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$, and descriptions of overrings as intersections of localisations are treated there.
- [[sheaves]] and [[algebraic-varieties]]: the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ of a variety at a point is a localisation of its coordinate ring, and the germ picture of the local ring at a point is the stalk of a sheaf.
- [[homological-algebra]] and [[tor]]: flatness of $S^{-1}A$, and projective and global dimension computed locally, are the starting point of Guan and Hu's formalisation of the Auslander-Buchsbaum-Serre criterion.
- Associated primes and regular sequences (a page in preparation) will treat how associated primes and regular sequences behave under localisation, and why $A \to A_{\mathfrak p}$ is flat but rarely faithfully flat.
- [[p-adic-numbers]]: the $p$-adic integers are the completion of $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$, the "more local" object described in the views on locality.
